reference_research_study_list.title: Beyond log-concavity: Provable guarantees for sampling multi-modal distributions using simulated tempering Langevin Monte Carlo.
reference_research_study_list.abstract:
A key task in Bayesian statistics is sampling from distributions that are
only specified up to a partition function (i.e., constant of proportionality).
However, without any assumptions, sampling (even approximately) can be #P-hard,
and few works have provided "beyond worst-case" guarantees for such settings.
  For log-concave distributions, classical results going back to Bakry and
\'Emery (1985) show that natural continuous-time Markov chains called Langevin
diffusions mix in polynomial time. The most salient feature of log-concavity
violated in practice is uni-modality: commonly, the distributions we wish to
sample from are multi-modal. In the presence of multiple deep and
well-separated modes, Langevin diffusion suffers from torpid mixing.
  We address this problem by combining Langevin diffusion with simulated
tempering. The result is a Markov chain that mixes more rapidly by
transitioning between different temperatures of the distribution. We analyze
this Markov chain for the canonical multi-modal distribution: a mixture of
gaussians (of equal variance). The algorithm based on our Markov chain provably
samples from distributions that are close to mixtures of gaussians, given
access to the gradient of the log-pdf. For the analysis, we use a spectral
decomposition theorem for graphs (Gharan and Trevisan, 2014) and a Markov chain
decomposition technique (Madras and Randall, 2002).

reference_research_study_list.title: Eldan’s stochastic localization and the KLS hyperplane conjecture: an improved lower bound for expansion.
reference_research_study_list.abstract:
We show that the Cheeger constant for $n$-dimensional isotropic logconcave
measures is $O(n^{1/4})$, improving on the previous best bound of
$O(n^{1/3}\sqrt{\log n}).$ As corollaries we obtain the same improved bound on
the thin-shell estimate, Poincar\'{e} constant and Lipschitz concentration
constant and an alternative proof of this bound for the isotropic (slicing)
constant; it also follows that the ball walk for sampling from an isotropic
logconcave density in ${\bf R}^{n}$ converges in $O^{*}(n^{2.5})$ steps from a
warm start. The proof is based on gradually transforming any logconcave density
to one that has a significant Gaussian factor via a Martingale process.
  Extending this proof technique, we prove that the log-Sobolev constant of any
isotropic logconcave density in ${\bf R}^{n}$ with support of diameter $D$ is
$\Omega(1/D)$, resolving a question posed by Frieze and Kannan in 1997. This is
asymptotically the best possible estimate and improves on the previous bound of
$\Omega(1/D^{2})$ by Kannan-Lov\'{a}sz-Montenegro. It follows that for any
isotropic logconcave density, the ball walk with step size
$\delta=\Theta(1/\sqrt{n})$ mixes in $O\left(n^{2}D\right)$ proper steps from
\emph{any }starting point. This improves on the previous best bound of
$O(n^{2}D^{2})$ and is also asymptotically tight.
  The new bound leads to the following large deviation inequality for an
$L$-Lipschitz function $g$ over an isotropic logconcave density $p$: for any
$t>0$, \[ Pr_{x\sim p}\left(\left|g(x)-\bar{g}\right|\geq L\cdot
t\right)\leq\exp(-\frac{c\cdot t^{2}}{t+\sqrt{n}}) \] where $\bar{g}$ is the
median or mean of $g$ for $x\sim p$; this generalizes and improves on previous
bounds by Paouris and by Guedon-Milman. The technique also bounds the ``small
ball'' probability in terms of the Cheeger constant, and recovers the current
best bound.

As corollaries we obtain the same improved bound on the thin-shell estimate, Poincarï¿œ constant and L ipschitz concentration constant and an alternative proof of this bound for the isotropic (slicing) constant; it also follows that the ball walk for sampling from an isotropic logconcave density in Rn converges in O∗ (n2.5) steps from a warm start. The proof is based on gradually transforming any logconcave den sity to one that has a signiﬁcant Gaussian factor via a Martingale process. Extending this proof technique, we prove that the log-Sobol ev constant of any isotropic logconcave density in Rn with support of diameter D is Ω(1 /D ), resolving a question posed by F rieze and Kannan in 1997. This is asymptotically the best possible estimate and improves on the previous bound of Ω(1 /D 2 ) by Kannan-Lovï¿œsz-Montenegro. It follows that for any iso tropic logconcave density, the ball walk with step size δ = Θ(1 / √ n) mixes in O ( n2D ) proper steps from any starting point. This improves on the previous best bound of O(n2D2) and is also asymptotically tight. The new bound leads to the following large deviation inequal ity for an L-Lipschitz function g over an isotropic logconcave density p: for any t > 0, Px∼ p (|g(x) − ¯g| ≥ L ·t) ≤ exp(− c ·t2 t + √ n ) where ¯g is the median or mean of g for x ∼ p; this generalizes and improves on previous bounds by Paouris and by Guedon-Milman. The technique also bounds the “small ball” probability in terms of the Cheeger constant, and recovers the current best bound. 1 Introduction In this paper we study the Cheeger constant and the log-Sobolev constant of logconcave measures in n- dimensional Euclidean space. These fundamental parameter s, which we will deﬁne presently , have many important connections and applications (cf. [ 32, 11]). The isoperimetry of a subset is the ratio of the measure of the boundary of the subset to the measure of the subset or its complement, whichever is smaller. The mini mum such ratio over all subsets is the Cheeger constant, also called expansion or isoperimetric coeﬃcien t. This fundamental constant appears in many settings, e.g., graphs and convex bodies, and plays an essen tial role in many lines of study . 1.1 Cheeger constant In the geometric setting, the KLS hyperplane conjecture [ 24] asserts that for any distribution with a log- concave density , the minimum expansion is approximated by t hat of a halfspace, up to a universal constant ∗ This update uniﬁes the results from [ 36] and [ 35]. † University of W ashington and Microsoft Research, yintat@u w.edu ‡ Georgia T ech, vempala@gatech.edu 0factor. Thus, if the conjecture is true, the Cheeger constan t can be essentially determined simply by exam- ining hyperplane cuts. More precisely , here is the statemen t. W e use c,C for absolute constants, a ≲ b to denote a≤ c· b for some absolute constant c, and ∥A∥op for the spectral/operator norm of a matrix A. Conjecture 1 ([24]). For any logconcave density p in Rn with covariance matrix A, 1 ψp def = inf S⊆Rn ∫ ∂S p(x)dx min {∫ S p(s)dx, ∫ Rn\S p(x)dx } ≳ 1√ ∥A∥op . F or an isotropic logconcave density (all eigenvalues of its covariance matrix are equal to 1), the conjectured isoperimetric ratio is an absolute constant. Note that the K LS constant ψp is the reciprocal of the Cheeger constant (this will be more convenient for comparisons with other constants). The conjecture was formulated by Kannan, Lovász and Simonovits in the course of their study of the convergence of a random process (the ball walk) in a convex body . They proved the following weaker bound. Theorem 2 ([24]). For any logconcave density pin Rn with covariance matrix A, the KLS constant satisﬁes ψp ≲ √ Tr(A). F or an isotropic distribution, the theorem gives a bound of O(√n), while the conjecture says O(1). The conjecture has several important consequences. F or exampl e, it implies that the ball walk mixes in O∗ ( n2) steps from a warm start in any isotropic convex body (or logco ncave density) in Rn; this is the best possible bound, and is tight e.g., for a hypercube. The KLS conjecture has become central to modern asymptotic convex geometry . It is equivalent to a bound on the spectral g ap of isotropic logconcave functions [ 30]. Although it was formulated due to an algorithmic motivation , it implies several well-known conjectures in asymptotic convex geometry . W e describe these next. The thin-shell conjecture (also known as the variance hypothesis) [43, 8] says the following. Conjecture 3 (Thin-shell). For a random point X from an isotropic logconcave density p in Rn, σ2 p def = E((∥X∥ − √n)2) ≲ 1. It implies that a random point X from an isotropic logconcave density lies in a constant-wid th annulus (a thin shell) with constant probability . Noting that σ2 p = E((∥X∥ − √n)2) ≤ 1 nVar(∥X∥2) ≲ σ2 p, the conjecture is equivalent to asserting that Var(∥X∥2) ≲ n for an isotropic logconcave density . The following connection is well-known: σp ≲ ψp. The current best bound is σp ≲ n 1 3 by Guedon and Milman [23], improving on a line of work that started with Klartag [ 28, 29, 20]. Eldan [ 16] has shown that the reverse inequality holds approximately , in a worst-case se nse, namely the worst possible KLS constant over all isotropic logconcave densities in Rn is bounded by the thin-shell estimate to within roughly a log arithmic factor in the dimension. This yields the current best bound o f ψp ≲ n 1 3 √log n. A weaker inequality was shown earlier by Bobkov [ 7] (see also [ 44]). The slicing conjecture, also called the hyperplane conjecture [10, 5] is the following. Conjecture 4 (Slicing/Isotropic constant) . Any convex body of unit volume in Rn contains a hyperplane section of at least constant volume. Equivalently, for any c onvex body K of unit volume with covariance matrix L2 KI, the isotropic constant LK ≲ 1. The isotropic constant of a general isotropic logconcave de nsity p is deﬁned as Lp = p(0)1/n. The best current bound is Lp ≲ n1/4, due to Klartag [ 27], improving on Bourgain’s bound of Lp ≲ n1/4 log n[9]. The study of this conjecture has played an inﬂuential role in the development of convex geometry over the past several decades. It was shown by Ball that the KLS conjecture implies the slicing conjecture. More recently , Eldan and Klartag [ 17] showed that the thin shell conjecture implies slicing, and therefore an alternative (and stronger) proof that KLS implies slicing: Lp ≲ σp ≲ ψp. Here are a few applications of the KLS bound. 1Theorem 5 (Poincaré constant [ 50, 12]). For any isotropic logconcave density p in Rn and any smooth function g, we have Varx∼pg(x) ≲ ψ2 p · Ex∼p ∥∇g(x)∥2 2. The Cheeger and log-Sobolev constants also play an importan t role in the phenomenon known as con- centration of measure. The following result is due to Gromov and Milman. Theorem 6 (Lipschitz concentration [ 22]). For any L-Lipschitz function g in Rn, and isotropic logconcave density p, Px∼p (|g(x) − Eg| ≥ ψp · L· t) ≤ e−c·t. A diﬀerent bound, independent of the Cheeger constant, for t he deviation in length of a random vector was given in a celebrated paper by Paouris [ 46] and improved by Guedon and Milman [ 23] (Paouris’ result has only the second term in the minimum below, and is sharp whe n t≳ √n). Theorem 7 ([23, 46]). For any isotropic logconcave density p, Px∼p (⏐ ⏐∥x∥ − √ n ⏐ ⏐≥ t ) ≤ e −c·min { t3 n ,t } . Our tight log-Sobolev bound will be useful in proving an impr oved concentration inequality . Finally , the Cheeger constant is useful for proving a central limit theor em for convex sets. Theorem 8 (Central Limit Theorem [ 43]). Let K be an isotropic symmetric convex set. Let gθ(s) = vol(K∩ { xT θ = s}) and g(s) = 1√ 2π exp(− s2 2 ). There are universal constants c1, c2 > 0 such that for any δ >0, we have vol ({ θ∈ Sn−1 : ⏐ ⏐ ⏐ ⏐ ∫ t −t gθ(s)ds− ∫ t −t g(s)ds ⏐ ⏐ ⏐ ⏐≤ c1(δ+ ψK √n) for every t∈ R }) ≥ 1 − ne−c2δ2n. F or more background on these conjectures, we refer the reade r to [ 11, 2, 3]. 1.2 Log-Sobolev constant The KLS conjecture was motivated by the study of the convergence of a Markov chain, the ball walk in a convex body . T o sample uniformly from a convex body , the ball walk starts at some point in the body , picks a random point in the ball of radius δ around the current point and if the chosen point is in the body , it steps to the new point. It can be generalized to sampling any l ogconcave density by using a Metropolis ﬁlter. As shown in [ 25], the ball walk applied to a logconcave density mixes in O∗(n2ψ2 p) steps from a warm start, which using the current-best bound [ 36] is O∗(n2.5). Looking closer, from a starting distribution Qo, the distance of the distribution obtained after t steps from Qo to the stationary distribution Q drops as d(Qt,Q) ≤ d(Q0,Q) ( 1 − φ2 2 )t where φis the conductance of the Markov chain and d(.,.) is the χ-squared distance. The conductance can be viewed as the Cheeger constant of the Markov chain. Thus the n umber of steps needed is O(φ−2 log(1/d(Q0,Q))). Roughly speaking, for the ball walk applied to a logconcave d ensity p, the conductance is Ω(1 /(nψp)), leading to the bound of O∗(n2ψ2 p) steps from a warm start. The dependence on the starting distr ibution leads to an additional factor of nin the running time when the starting distribution is not war m (i.e., d(Q1,Q) after one step can be e−Ω( n) ). This is a general issue for Markov chains. One way to addres s this is via the log-Sobolev constant [ 15, 32]. W e ﬁrst deﬁne it for a density , then for a Markov chain. Deﬁnition 9. F or a density p, the log-Sobolev constant ρp is the largest ρ such that for every smooth function f : Rn → R with ∫ f2dp= 1 , we have ρ 2 ∫ f2 log f2dp≤ ∫ ∥∇f∥2 dp. 2A closely related parameter is the following. Deﬁnition 10. The log-Cheeger constant κp of a density p in Rn is κp = inf S⊆Rn p(∂S) min {p(S),p(Rn \ S)} √ log ( 1 p(S) ). It is known that ρp = Θ( κ2 p) (see e.g., [ 31]). The log-Cheeger constant shows more explicitly that the log-Sobolev constant is a uniform bound on the expansion “at every scale”. F or a reversible Markov chain with transition operator P and stationary density Q, we can deﬁne the log-Sobolev constant ρ(P) be the largest ρ such that for every smooth functions satisfying f : Rn → R with∫ f2dp= 1 , we have ρ 2 ∫ f2 log f2dQ≤ ∫ x ∫ y ∥f(x) − f(y)∥2 P(x,y)dQ(x). Diaconis and Saloﬀ-Coste [ 15] show that the distribution after tsteps satisﬁes Ent(Qt) ≤ e−c·ρ(P )t · Ent(Q0) where Ent(Qt) = ∫ Qt log Qt Q0 dQ0 is the entropy with respect to the stationary distribution. Thus, the depen- dence of the mixing time on the starting distribution goes do wn from log(1/d(Q0,Q)) to log log(1/d(Q0,Q))). Moreover, just as in the case of the Cheeger constant, for the ball walk, the Markov chain parameter is deter- mined by the log-Sobelov constant ρp for sampling from the density p (See Theorem 18). It is thus natural to ask for the best possible bound on ρp or κp. Unlike the Cheeger constant, which is conjectured to be at least a constant for isotropic logconcave densities, it is k nown that ρp cannot be bounded from below by a universal constant, in particular for distributions that a re not “ ψ2” (distributions with sub-Gaussian tail). Kannan, Lovász and Montenegro [ 26] gave the following bound on κp. Our main result (Theorem 15) is an improvement of this bound to the best possible when the dis tribution is isotropic. Theorem 11 ([26]). For a logconcave density K ⊂ Rn with support of diameter D, we have κp ≳ 1 D and ρp ≳ 1 D2 . F rom the above bound, it follows that the ball walk mixes in O ( n2D2) proper steps of step size δ= Θ( 1√n ). A proper step is one where the current point changes. F or an is otropic logconcave density δ= Θ( 1√n ) is small enough so that the number of wasted steps is of the same order a s the number of proper steps in expectation. Moreover, by restricting to a ball of radius D= O(√n), the resulting distribution remains near-isotropic and very close in total variation distance to the original. T oge ther, this considerations imply a bound of O∗(n3) proper steps from any starting point as shown in [ 26]. Is this bound the best possible? F rom a warm start, the KLS conjecture implies a bound of O∗(n2) steps and current best bound is O∗(n2.5). Thus, the mixing of the ball walk, which was the primary motivation for formul ation of the KLS conjecture, also provides a compelling reason to study the log-Sobolev constant. More generally , for any distribution whose density function is the product of the Gaussian density for N(0,σ2I) and any logconcave function, it is known that the expansion is Ω (1/σ) [ 13]. This fact is used crucially in the Gaussian cooling algori thm of [ 14] for computing the volume of a convex body by starting with a st andard Gaussian restricted to a convex body and gradually making the variance of the Gaussian large enough that it is eﬀectively uniform over the convex body of interest. Our overall strategy is similar in spirit — we start with an arbitrary isotropic logconcave density and gradually introduce a Gaussian term in the density of smaller and smaller variance. The isoperimetry of the resulting distribution after suﬃci ent time will be very good since it has a large Gaussian factor. And crucially , it can be related to the isop erimetry of the initial distribution. T o achieve the latter, we would like to maintain the measure of a ﬁxed sub set close to its initial value as the distribution changes. F or this, our proof uses the localization approach to proving high-dimensional inequalities [ 39, 24], and in particular, the elegant stochastic version introduc ed by Eldan [ 16] and used in subsequent papers [19, 18]. W e ﬁx a subset E of the original space with measure one half according to the o riginal logconcave dis- tribution (it suﬃces to consider such subsets to bound the is operimetric constant). In standard localization, we then repeatedly bisect space using a hyperplane that pres erves the volume fraction of E. The limit of this process is a partition into 1-dimensional logconcave measu res (“needles”), for which inequalities are much easier to prove. This approach runs into major diﬃculties fo r proving the KLS conjecture. While the original measure might be isotropic, the 1-dimensional measures cou ld, in principle, have variances roughly equal to the trace of the original covariance (i.e., long thin needle s), for which only much weaker inequalities hold. Stochastic localization can be viewed as the continuous tim e version of this process, where at each step, we pick a random direction and multiply the current density wit h a linear function along the chosen direction. Over time, the density can be viewed as a spherical Gaussian t imes a logconcave function, with the Gaussian gradually reducing in variance. When the Gaussian becomes s uﬃciently small in variance, then the overall distribution has good isoperimetric coeﬃcient, determine d by the inverse of the Gaussian standard deviation (such an inequality can be shown using standard localizatio n, as in [ 13]). An important property of the inﬁnitesimal change at each step is balance – the density at time tis a martingale and therefore the expected measure of any subset is the same as the original measure. Ove r time, the measure of a set E is a random quantity that deviates from its original value of 1 2 over time. The main question then is: what direction to use at each step so that (a) the measure of E remains bounded and (b) the Gaussian part of the density has small variance. W e show that the simplest choice, namely a pure random direction chosen from the uniform distribution suﬃces. The analysis needs a potentia l function that grows slowly but still maintains good control over the spectral norm of the current covarianc e matrix. The direct choice of ∥At∥op, where At is the covariance matrix of the distribution at time t, is hard to control. W e use Tr(A2 t). This gives us the improved bound of O(n1/4). 1.5 Approach for log-Sobolev constant: Stieltjes potentia l W e apply the localization process to bound the log-Sobolev c onstant. reference_research_study_list.title: Convergence rate of Riemannian Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and faster polytope volume computation.
reference_research_study_list.abstract:
We give the first rigorous proof of the convergence of Riemannian Hamiltonian
Monte Carlo, a general (and practical) method for sampling Gibbs distributions.
Our analysis shows that the rate of convergence is bounded in terms of natural
smoothness parameters of an associated Riemannian manifold. We then apply the
method with the manifold defined by the log barrier function to the problems of
(1) uniformly sampling a polytope and (2) computing its volume, the latter by
extending Gaussian cooling to the manifold setting. In both cases, the total
number of steps needed is O^{*}(mn^{\frac{2}{3}}), improving the state of the
art. A key ingredient of our analysis is a proof of an analog of the KLS
conjecture for Gibbs distributions over manifolds.

The Hamiltonian H, which captures jointly the potential and kinetic energy of a particle, is a function of its position and velocity . First-order diﬀerential equations describe the change in both. dx dt = ∂H(x,v) ∂v , dv dt = −∂H(x,v) ∂x . As we review in Section 2, these equations preserve the Hamiltonian H. Riemannian Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (or RHMC) [ 26, 25][6, 7] is a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method for sampling from a desired distribution. The target distribution is encoded in the deﬁnition of the Hamiltonian. Each step of the method consists of the fo llowing: At a current point x, 1. Pick a random velocity yaccording to a local distribution deﬁned by x(in the simplest setting, this is the standard Gaussian distribution for every x). 2. Move along the Hamiltonian curve deﬁned by Hamiltonian dy namics at (x,y) for time (dis- tance) δ. F or a suitable choice of H, the marginal distribution of the current point x approaches the desired target distribution. Conceptually , the main advantage of R HMC is that it does not require a Metropolis ﬁlter (as in the Metropolis-Hastings method) an d its step sizes are therefore not severely limited even in high dimension. Over the past two decades, RHMC has become very popular in Sta tistics and Machine Learning, being applied to Bayesian learning, to evaluate expectation s and likelihood of large models by sam- pling from the appropriate Gibbs distribution, etc. It has b een reported to signiﬁcantly outperform other known methods [ 2, 25] and much eﬀort has been made to make each step eﬃcient by the u se of numerical methods for solving ODEs. In spite of all these developments and the remarkable empiri cal popularity of RHMC, analyzing its rate of convergence and thus rigorously explaining its s uccess has remained an open question. 1.1 Results In this paper, we analyze the mixing rate of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for a general function f as a Gibbs sampler, i.e., to generate samples from the density pr oportional to e−f(x). The corresponding Hamiltonian is H(x,v) = f(x) + 1 2 log((2π)n det g(x)) + 1 2 vT g(x)−1v for some metric g. W e show that for x in a compact manifold, the conductance of the Markov chain is bounded in terms of a few parameters of the metric g and the function f. The parameters and resulting bounds are given in Corollary 28 and Theorem 30. Roughly speaking, the guarantee says that Hamiltonian Monte Carlo mixes in polynomial time for smooth Hamiltonian s. W e note that these guarantees use only the smoothness and Cheeger constant (expansion) of the function, without any convexity type assumptions. Thus, they might provide insight in nonco nvex settings where (R)HMC is often applied. W e then focus on logconcave densities in Rn, i.e., f(x) is a convex function. This class of functions appears naturally in many contexts and is known to be sampleable in polynomial-time given access to a function value oracle. F or logconcave dens ities, the current fastest sampling algorithms use n4 function calls, even for uniform sampling [ 20, 23], and n2.5 oracle calls given a 3warm start after appropriate rounding (linear transformat ion) [ 14]. In the prototypical setting of uniform sampling from a polytope Ax≥ b, with minequalities, the general complexity is no better, with each function evaluation taking O(mn) arithmetic operations, for an overall complexity of n4 · mn = mn5 in the worst case and n2.5 · mn after rounding from a warm start. The work of Kannan and Narayanan [ 11] gives an algorithm of complexity mn2 · mnω−1 from an arbitrary start and mn· mnω−1 from a warm start (here ω is the matrix multiplication exponent), which is better than the general case when the number of facets m is not too large. This was recently improved to mn0.75 · mnω−1 from a warm start [ 13]; the subquadratic complexity for the number of steps is signiﬁcant since all known general oracle methods cannot be low a quadratic number of steps. The leading algorithms and their guarantees are summarized in T able 1. The entries marked # are for general convex bodies presented by oracles, while the rest are for polytopes. In this paper, using RHMC, we improve the complexity of sampl ing polytopes. In fact we do this for a general family of Gibbs distributions, of the form e−αφ(x) where φ(x) is a convex function over a polytope. When φ(x) is the standard logarithmic barrier function and g(x) is its Hessian, we get a sampling method that mixes in only n 1 6 m 1 2 + n 1 5 m 2 5 α 1 5 +m− 1 5 + n 2 3 α+m−1 steps from a warm start! When α= 1 /m, the resulting distribution is very close to uniform over th e polytope. Theorem 1. Let φ be the logarithmic barrier for a polytope M with m constraints and n variables. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo applied to the function f = exp( −αφ(x)) and the metric given by ∇2φ with appropriate step size mixes in ˜O ( n 2 3 α+ m−1 + m 1 3 n 1 3 α 1 3 + m− 1 3 + m 1 2 n 1 6 ) steps where each step is the solution of a Hamiltonian ODE. In recent independent work, Mangoubi and Smith [ 24] analyze Euclidean HMC in the oracle set- ting, i.e., assuming an oracle for evaluating φ. Their analysis formally gives a dimension-independent convergence rate based on certain regularity assumptions s uch as strong convexity and smoothness of the Hamiltonian H. Unfortunately , these assumptions do not hold for the polyt ope sampling problem. An important application of sampling is integration. The co mplexity of integration for general logconcave functions is also n4 oracle calls. F or polytopes, the most natural questions is c omputing its volume. F or this problem, the current best complexity is n4 · mn, where the factor of O(mn) is the complexity of checking membership in a polytope. While this l eads to polynomial-time convergence for logconcave distributions, the length of each step has to be s mall due to boundary eﬀects, and a Metropolis ﬁlter (rejection sampling) has to be applied to e nsure the limiting distribution is the desired one. These walks cannot aﬀord a step of length greate r than δ= O ( 1 √n ) for a distribution in isotropic position, and take a quadratic number of steps e ven for the hypercube. The Dikin walk for polytopes [ 11], which explicitly takes into account the boundary of polyt ope at each step, has a varying step size, but still runs into similar issues and the bound on its convergence rate is O(mn) for a polytope with mfacets. 1We suspect that the LS barrier [ 12] might be used to get a faster algorithm even in the regime eve n if m is sub-exponential. Rather than using straig ht lines in Euclidean space, each step of the walk is along a geodesic (lo cally shortest path) of a Riemannian metric. More precisely , each step ﬁrst makes a deterministi c move depending on the current point (drift), then moves along a geodesic in a random initial dire ction and ﬁnally uses a Metropolis ﬁlter. Each step can be computed by solving a ﬁrst-order ODE. Due to t he combination of drift and geodesic, the local 1-step distributions are smoother than that of the Dikin walk and larger steps can be taken while keeping a bounded rejection probability f or the ﬁlter. F or sampling polytopes, the manifold/metric deﬁned by the standard log barrier give s a convergence rate of mn 3 4 , going below the quadratic (or higher) bound of all previous sampli ng methods. One major diﬃculty with geodesic walk is ensuring the statio nary distribution is uniform. F or high dimensional problems, this necessitates taking a suﬃc iently small step size and then rejecting some samples according to the desired transition probabili ties according to Metropolis ﬁlter. Un- fortunately , computing these transition probabilities ca n be very expensive. F or the geodesic walk, it entails solving an n× n size matrix ODE. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo bears some similarity to the geodes ic walk — each step is a random (non-linear) curve. But the Hamiltonian-preserving nature of the process obviates the most expen- sive ingredient, Metropolis ﬁlter. Due to this, the step siz e can be made longer, and as a result we obtain a faster sampling algorithm for polytopes that mixes in mn 2 3 steps (the per-step complexity remains essentially the same, needing the solution of an ODE ). T o get a faster algorithm for volume computation, we extends the analysis to a general family of Gibbs distributions, including f(x) = e−αφ(x) where φ(x) is the standard log-barrier and α> 0. W e show that the smoothness we need for the sampling correspond ing to a variant of self-concordance deﬁned in Deﬁnition 46. F urthermore, we establish an isoperimetric inequality fo r this class of functions. This can be viewed as an extension of the KLS hyper plane conjecture from Euclidean to Riemannian metrics (the analogous case in Euclidean space t o what we prove here is the isoperimetry of the Gaussian density function multiplied by any logconca ve function, a case for which the KLS conjecture holds). The mixing rate for this family of functi ons is sublinear for α= Ω(1) . Finally , we study the Gaussian Cooling schedule of [ 3]. W e show that in the manifold setting, the Gaussian distribution e−∥x∥2/2 can be replaced by e−αφ(x). Moreover, the speed of Gaussian Cooling depends on the “thin-shell” constant of the manifol d and classical self-concordance of φ. Combining all of these ideas, we obtain a faster algorithm fo r polytope volume computation. The resulting complexity of polytope volume computation is the same as that of sampling uniformly from a warm start: mn 2 3 steps. T o illustrate the improvement, for polytopes with m= O(n) facets, the new bound is n 5 3 while the previous best bound was n4. 1.3 Practicality F rom the experiments, the ball walk/hit-and-run seem to mixin n2 steps, the geodesic walk seems to mix in sublinear number of steps (due to the Metropolis ﬁlt er bottleneck) and RHMC seems to mix in only polylogarithmic number of steps. One advantage o f RHMC compared to the geodesic walk is that it does not require the expensive Metropolis ﬁlt er that involves solving n× n matrix ODEs. In the future, we plan to do an empirical comparison stu dy of diﬀerent sampling algorithms. new_method.method:
Open Problems: Per-step redundant computation.  Current accelerators (early–exit, token–merge, encoder-propagation, etc.) prove that successive denoising steps reuse most intermediate information, yet they all treat the backbone as a static feed-forward UNet that must be executed (wholly or partly) every step.  Skipping or caching layers saves FLOPs but either (i) forces heavy memory traffic to store / fetch feature pyramids, (ii) requires manual schedules, or (iii) degrades quality for very-few-step samplers.  What is still missing is an architecture that is natively time-recurrent: it should compute a rich feature hierarchy once and update it with lightweight, learnable "delta" operations at later timesteps, eliminating both redundant FLOPs and large feature caches.  Solving this would give order-of-magnitude speedups while remaining sampler-agnostic and memory friendly.
Methods: 1. Recurrent Residual Diffusion Network (R2Diff).
   a) One-Time Encoder (OTE): at the first denoising step t0 the full multi-scale encoder (identical to SD-UNet / DiT encoder) is run, producing hidden states H^l_0 at all resolutions l.
   b) Recurrent Delta Modules (RDM): for every later step t_k the encoder is replaced by cheap, weight-shared Δ-blocks that update hidden states:  H^l_k = H^l_{k-1} + Δ^l(H^l_{k-1}, t_k, g_k) where g_k is the global latent/noise embedding.  Each Δ-block is a depth-wise ConvGRU + FiLM layer (≈10× cheaper than the original ResNet+Attention pair).
   c) Lightweight Decoder Reuse: the original decoder is kept, but its key-frame features come from the current H^l_k.  Because Δs are small, gradients flow through time easily; checkpointing is unnecessary during inference.
   d) Training: unroll K random steps per iteration (K∈[2,6]), sample a start-step s∼U(0,T−K), and minimize standard epsilon/v-prediction loss at all unrolled timesteps.  Teacher forcing from a pretrained UNet (moment-matching distillation) is added for stability.
   e) Timestep-Adaptive Budget: a learned gating scalar γ_k per layer (produced by a tiny MLP of t_k) modulates Δ-block compute; near prior (large t) γ_k→0, saving even more FLOPs—this replaces manual early-exit schedules.
   f) Memory-Aware Quantized State: hidden states are stored in 8-bit uint with per-channel scale; Δ-blocks operate in FP16 and output 8-bit-quantized results, cutting SRAM/BW cost.
   g) Compatibility: R2Diff is orthogonal to fast samplers (DDIM, DPM-Solver, LCM) and to other tricks (PTQ4DM, ToMe in the first OTE pass, RTK large steps, etc.).
Experimental Setup: Backbones & datasets:
• Stable Diffusion v1.5 UNet (latent 64×64) – MS-COCO 2014 captions (30k prompts) for FID/CLIP; LAION-Aesthetics 2M for fine-tuning.
• DiT-XL/2 (256²) – ImageNet-256 class-conditional.
Samplers: DDPM-50, DDIM-25, DPM-Solver++-15, LCM-8.
Baselines: original model, FasterDiffusion (encoder propagation), ASE, ToMe (0.4), SnapFusion-8-step, LCM-SD15.
Metrics:
1. Quality – FID (50k samples), CLIP-score, precision/recall.
2. Efficiency – images/s, average latency on A100 and iPhone-14-Pro (CoreML), GPU energy (nvidia-smi), peak memory.
3. Robustness – performance when (a) varying #steps 5-50, (b) strong CFG 1-15, (c) high-resolution 1024².
Ablations: (i) Δ-block depth (1 vs 2 convGRU layers), (ii) 4-bit vs 8-bit state, (iii) learned vs manual γ_k, (iv) distillation vs full scratch training.
Statistical sign.: 3 seeds, report mean±std.
Result: Expected--Compared to original UNet: 
• 3.2× speedup (GPU), 4.5× on mobile; 55 % lower energy; peak mem −40 %.
• FID degradation ≤0.15 on COCO (SD15-DDIM-25), parity on ImageNet-256 (DiT-DDPM-50); in very-few-step regime (≤8) R2Diff outperforms Encoder-Propagation and ASE by 0.5-1.0 FID.
• Learned γ_k automatically prunes ≥60 % of Δ-block FLOPs for t>0.7T.
• Quantized state yields <0.02 FID loss while saving 30 % mem bw.
• Compatible with LCM-8: maintains FID 7.8 vs 7.9 baseline but 2× faster.
Conclusion: R2Diff turns diffusion backbones into time-recurrent networks, eliminating redundant per-step computation instead of merely skipping or caching it.  The prototype shows multi-fold speedups with negligible quality loss, is sampler-agnostic, memory-efficient and friendly to edge hardware.  Academically, it opens a new design axis—stateful feature evolution—for generative diffusion, bridging ideas from RNNs and iterative vision transformers.  Practically, it enables sub-second 1024² image generation on a single smartphone GPU, paving the way for real-time interactive applications.  Future work: joint training with RTK one-shot samplers, neural architecture search for optimal Δ-blocks, and extending the recurrent paradigm to video and 3D diffusion.

experimental_design.experiment_strategy:
Title: Validating R2Diff: a time-recurrent diffusion backbone that eliminates per-step redundant computation

Overview: The three experiments below are designed to jointly validate speed, memory, and quality benefits of R2Diff, its sampler-agnostic robustness, and the contribution of each component (Δ-blocks, state quantization, learned gating, distillation). All experiments are implementable in Python (PyTorch), with optional on-device measurement using Core ML.

----------------------------------------------------------------
Experiment 1 — End-to-end speed, memory, energy, and quality on SD1.5 (COCO/LAION) with DDIM-25

Goal:
- Demonstrate R2Diff’s speedup, memory reduction, energy savings, and near-parity image quality relative to the original UNet across typical 25-step sampling.
- Quantify learned gating γk and 8-bit state benefits.

Models and data:
- Base: Stable Diffusion v1.5 UNet (latent 64×64). Pretrained weights for the backbone.
- Train R2Diff using the same VAE/text encoder as SD1.5; replace encoder with OTE+RDM and reuse the original decoder.
- Training: LAION-Aesthetics subset (e.g., 2M as in plan; for feasibility, start with 200k–500k samples), captions via CLIP-ViT-L/14 tokenizer.
- Evaluation: MS-COCO 2014 val prompts (30k) for FID/CLIP/prec-recall.

Baselines:
- Original UNet (same sampler and steps).
- Encoder propagation baseline (e.g., FasterDiffusion or similar open-source implementation).
- ASE and ToMe(0.4) applied to the baseline.

Training recipe:
- Unroll K∈[2,6] steps per iteration, s~Uniform(0, T−K).
- Standard ε-pred loss at all unrolled steps; optionally v-pred variant.
- Teacher forcing from frozen SD1.5 UNet: L_distill = MSE(ε_pred_R2Diff, ε_pred_teacher) at unrolled steps.
- RDM: weight-shared Δ-blocks across time; γk gating per layer.
- State quantization: store hidden states as uint8 with per-channel scale; Δ-blocks FP16.
- Optimizer: AdamW (1e-4), β=(0.9, 0.95), wd=0.01. Cosine LR. 200k–400k steps warmup 2k.

Evaluation protocol:
- Sampler: DDIM-25 (primary), plus DDPM-50 for reference on smaller slice.
- Metrics: FID (50k), CLIP score, Precision/Recall, throughput (images/s), average latency, peak GPU memory, total GPU energy.
- Devices: A100-80GB (primary). Optional: iPhone-14-Pro (Core ML) for latency.
- Robustness sanity checks: steps ∈{8, 15, 25} and CFG ∈{3, 7.5, 12} on a 10k subset.
- 3 seeds; report mean±std.

Success criteria:
- >=3× speedup on A100; <=0.15 FID delta vs baseline on DDIM-25; ≥40% lower peak memory; ≥40% energy reduction; gating prunes >50% Δ-block FLOPs at large t.

Key implementation snippets (PyTorch):

1) Depthwise ConvGRU + FiLM Δ-block

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

class DepthwiseConvGRU(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, C, k=3):
        super().__init__()
        padding = k//2
        self.conv_z = nn.Conv2d(C*2, C, k, padding=padding, groups=C)  # depthwise
        self.conv_r = nn.Conv2d(C*2, C, k, padding=padding, groups=C)
        self.conv_h = nn.Conv2d(C*2, C, k, padding=padding, groups=C)
    def forward(self, x, h):
        if h is None:
            h = torch.zeros_like(x)
        xh = torch.cat([x, h], dim=1)
        z = torch.sigmoid(self.conv_z(xh))
        r = torch.sigmoid(self.conv_r(xh))
        rh = torch.cat([x, r*h], dim=1)
        h_tilde = torch.tanh(self.conv_h(rh))
        h_new = (1 - z) * h + z * h_tilde
        return h_new

class FiLM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, C, d_embed=512):
        super().__init__()
        self.proj = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(d_embed, 2*C),
            nn.SiLU(),
            nn.Linear(2*C, 2*C)
        )
    def forward(self, x, cond):
        # cond: time/noise embedding (batch, d_embed)
        gamma_beta = self.proj(cond)  # (B, 2C)
        gamma, beta = gamma_beta.chunk(2, dim=-1)
        gamma = gamma[..., None, None]
        beta = beta[..., None, None]
        return x * (1 + gamma) + beta

class DeltaBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, C, d_embed=512, depth=1):
        super().__init__()
        self.grus = nn.ModuleList([DepthwiseConvGRU(C) for _ in range(depth)])
        self.film = FiLM(C, d_embed)
        self.out = nn.Conv2d(C, C, 1)
    def forward(self, h_prev, cond):
        h = h_prev
        for gru in self.grus:
            h = gru(h_prev, h)  # residual state evolution
        h = self.film(h, cond)
        delta = self.out(h)
        return delta

2) Per-channel uint8 quantization for hidden states

class PerChannelUint8:
    @staticmethod
    def quantize(x):
        # x: (B, C, H, W), float16/float32
        x = x.float()
        B, C, H, W = x.shape
        x_flat = x.permute(0,2,3,1).reshape(-1, C)  # (B*H*W, C)
        min_c = x_flat.min(dim=0).values
        max_c = x_flat.max(dim=0).values
        scale = (max_c - min_c).clamp(min=1e-8) / 255.0
        zp = (-min_c / scale).round().clamp(0, 255)
        q = (x.permute(0,2,3,1) / scale - zp).round().clamp(0,255).byte()
        q = q.permute(0,3,1,2).contiguous()
        return q, scale, zp
    @staticmethod
    def dequantize(q, scale, zp):
        x = (q.float() + zp[None,:,None,None]) * scale[None,:,None,None]
        return x

3) Gating MLP producing γk in [0,1]

class TimeGating(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_embed):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(d_embed, d_embed//2), nn.SiLU(),
            nn.Linear(d_embed//2, 1), nn.Sigmoid()
        )
    def forward(self, t_embed):
        return self.net(t_embed).view(-1,1,1,1)  # broadcastable scalar per layer

4) R2Diff encoder replacement and recurrent inference

class R2DiffEncoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, sd15_encoder, channel_layout, d_embed=512, depth=1):
        super().__init__()
        self.ote = sd15_encoder  # run once at t0
        self.delta_blocks = nn.ModuleList([DeltaBlock(C, d_embed, depth) for C in channel_layout])
        self.gates = nn.ModuleList([TimeGating(d_embed) for _ in channel_layout])
    def run_ote(self, x0):
        # returns list of feature maps per scale
        with torch.no_grad():
            feats = self.ote(x0)
        return feats
    def recurrent_update(self, feats_q, scales, zps, cond_emb):
        # feats_q: list of uint8 tensors (per scale); scales/zps: lists of per-channel params
        new_feats_q, new_scales, new_zps = [], [], []
        for l,(q,sc,zp,db,gate) in enumerate(zip(feats_q, scales, zps, self.delta_blocks, self.gates)):
            h = PerChannelUint8.dequantize(q, sc.to(q.device), zp.to(q.device)).to(dtype=torch.float16)
            gamma = gate(cond_emb)  # (B,1,1,1)
            delta = db(h, cond_emb) * gamma
            h_new = (h + delta).to(dtype=torch.float32)
            q_new, sc_new, zp_new = PerChannelUint8.quantize(h_new)
            new_feats_q.append(q_new)
            new_scales.append(sc_new)
            new_zps.append(zp_new)
        return new_feats_q, new_scales, new_zps

# Inference loop sketch (DDIM-25):
# teacher text/cond embeddings omitted for brevity

def sample_ddim_r2diff(x_T, timesteps, text_cond, encoder, decoder, eps_head, time_embed_fn, global_embed_fn):
    # x_T: latent noise; timesteps: list[int], e.g., 25 to 0
    # encoder: R2DiffEncoder with OTE+Δ
    # decoder: original SD decoder that consumes current encoder features
    device = x_T.device
    x = x_T
    feats_q = scales = zps = None
    for i, t in enumerate(timesteps):
        t_embed = time_embed_fn(torch.tensor([t], device=device))  # (1, d_embed)
        g = global_embed_fn(x, t_embed, text_cond)  # (B, d_embed)
        cond_emb = g  # used by Δ-blocks and gating
        if i == 0:
            feats_fp = encoder.run_ote(x)  # list of float tensors per scale
            feats_q, scales, zps = [], [], []
            for h in feats_fp:
                q, sc, zp = PerChannelUint8.quantize(h)
                feats_q.append(q); scales.append(sc); zps.append(zp)
        else:
            feats_q, scales, zps = encoder.recurrent_update(feats_q, scales, zps, cond_emb)
        # Decode using current features (decoder should accept feature hooks or input adapters)
        h_current = [PerChannelUint8.dequantize(q, sc.to(device), zp.to(device)).to(dtype=torch.float16)
                     for q,sc,zp in zip(feats_q, scales, zps)]
        eps = eps_head(decoder(x, h_current), t_embed, text_cond)  # model epsilon
        # DDIM update step:
        x = ddim_update(x, eps, t)
    return x

5) Energy, throughput, and memory measurement

import time, pynvml, torch

def measure_run(fn, *args, warmup=3, repeat=10):
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    for _ in range(warmup):
        _ = fn(*args)
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
    times = []
    pynvml.nvmlInit()
    handle = pynvml.nvmlDeviceGetHandleByIndex(0)
    energies = []
    for _ in range(repeat):
        torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
        t0 = time.time()
        p0 = pynvml.nvmlDeviceGetPowerUsage(handle)  # mW
        y = fn(*args)
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        p1 = pynvml.nvmlDeviceGetPowerUsage(handle)
        t1 = time.time()
        times.append(t1 - t0)
        energies.append(((p0 + p1) / 2.0) * (t1 - t0) / 1e3)  # joules approx
        peak_mem = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / (1024**2)
    pynvml.nvmlShutdown()
    return {
        'latency_ms_mean': 1000*sum(times)/len(times),
        'latency_ms_std': 1000*torch.tensor(times).std().item(),
        'energy_j_mean': sum(energies)/len(energies),
        'peak_mem_mb': peak_mem
    }

6) FID/CLIP computation (torch-fidelity + open_clip)

# pip install torch-fidelity open-clip-torch
from torch_fidelity import calculate_metrics
import open_clip

def compute_fid(real_dir, gen_dir):
    metrics = calculate_metrics(input1=real_dir, input2=gen_dir, metrics=["fid"], verbose=False)
    return metrics["frechet_inception_distance"]

def compute_clip_score(imgs, texts, model="ViT-L-14"):  # imgs: list PIL; texts: list str
    model, _, preprocess = open_clip.create_model_and_transforms(model, pretrained='openai')
    model = model.eval().cuda()
    with torch.no_grad():
        imgs_t = torch.stack([preprocess(im).cuda() for im in imgs])
        tokens = open_clip.tokenize(texts).cuda()
        img_feat = model.encode_image(imgs_t)
        txt_feat = model.encode_text(tokens)
        img_feat = img_feat / img_feat.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        txt_feat = txt_feat / txt_feat.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        sim = (img_feat @ txt_feat.T).diag().mean().item()
    return sim

Notes:
- Hooking R2Diff into SD’s decoder: use feature hooks to feed h_current into the decoder’s skip connections at each scale (same tensor shapes as baseline encoder outputs).
- ToMe/ASE/FasterDiffusion baselines can be integrated from their public repos; standardize prompts and seeds.

----------------------------------------------------------------
Experiment 2 — Sampler-agnostic and cross-backbone generalization (SD1.5 and DiT-XL/2)

Goal:
- Show R2Diff is orthogonal to samplers and backbones.
- Verify parity on ImageNet-256 with DiT, and compatibility with fast samplers (e.g., LCM-8) on SD1.5.

Models and data:
- SD1.5: as in Exp1.
- DiT-XL/2 256×256: ImageNet-256 class-conditional (official split). Use class embeddings instead of text.

Samplers:
- DDPM-50, DDIM-25, DPM-Solver++-15, LCM-8.

Evaluation matrix:
- Steps: {5, 8, 15, 25, 50} (where applicable for the sampler).
- CFG: {1, 3, 7.5, 12, 15}.
- Metrics: FID (50k), Precision/Recall, CLIP score (for SD1.5), throughput, peak memory.

Protocol:
- For SD1.5: run the full grid across samplers and steps on 10k samples for pilot, then 50k for final.
- For DiT-XL/2: train R2Diff with One-Time Encoder set to DiT’s encoder block, RDMs per DiT stage. Evaluate FID on ImageNet-256 (50k).
- LCM compatibility: apply LCM distillation/weights for SD1.5 and plug R2Diff in place of the encoder; verify FID parity and speedup.

Success criteria:
- SD1.5: FID parity within ±0.15 at 25 steps across samplers; improved FID vs encoder-propagation and ASE at ≤8 steps; ≥2× speedup with LCM-8 maintaining FID.
- DiT-XL/2: FID parity to DiT baseline on DDPM-50, with ≥3× speedup.

Grid runner (Python):

Keep quantized state between steps. Decoder reuse corresponds to DiT’s final blocks that map back to image space.

----------------------------------------------------------------
Experiment 3 — Component ablations: Δ-depth, quantized state precision, gating strategy, and distillation

Goal:
- Isolate contributions of each component to quality and efficiency.

Factors:
- Δ-block depth: 1 vs 2 ConvGRU layers.
- State precision: 8-bit vs 4-bit uint; measure quality and memory/BW.
- Gating: learned γk vs manual schedule vs off.
- Distillation: with teacher forcing vs training from scratch.

Protocol:
- Train small runs (50k–100k steps) on LAION-A aesthetics subset and evaluate on 10k COCO prompts with DDIM-25 for quick iteration.
- After identifying promising settings, confirm on full 50k FID.
- Metrics: FID, CLIP, throughput, peak memory, GPU energy; FLOPs pruned by gating; gradient stability (loss curves, exploding/vanishing checks).

Success criteria:
- Δ-depth=1 matches quality of depth=2 with better speed.
- 8-bit state shows <0.02 FID loss vs float state; 4-bit shows modest degradation but significant memory/BW reduction.
- Learned γk outperforms manual schedule on FID and prunes ≥60% Δ-FLOPs at large t.
- Distillation stabilizes training and improves FID vs scratch.

Implementation helpers:

1) 4-bit quantization switch

class PerChannelUint4:
    @staticmethod
    def quantize(x):
        x = x.float()
        B,C,H,W = x.shape
        x_flat = x.permute(0,2,3,1).reshape(-1,C)
        min_c = x_flat.min(dim=0).values
        max_c = x_flat.max(dim=0).values
        scale = (max_c - min_c).clamp(min=1e-8) / 15.0
        zp = (-min_c / scale).round().clamp(0, 15)
        q = (x.permute(0,2,3,1) / scale - zp).round().clamp(0,15).to(torch.uint8)
        # pack two 4-bit into one byte if desired
        return q, scale, zp
    @staticmethod
    def dequantize(q, scale, zp):
        return (q.float() + zp[None,:,None,None]) * scale[None,:,None,None]

2) Manual schedule for γk for comparison

def manual_gamma(t, T, strategy='linear'):
    # t in [0,T]; smaller t -> later steps
    if strategy == 'linear':
        return max(0.0, min(1.0, 1.0 - t/T))
    if strategy == 'piecewise':
        return 0.0 if t > 0.7*T else (0.5 if t > 0.4*T else 1.0)

3) FLOP counting for Δ-blocks and gating effectiveness

# pip install fvcore
from fvcore.nn import FlopCountAnalysis

def measure_flops_delta_block(delta_block, h_prev, cond_emb):
    fca = FlopCountAnalysis(delta_block, (h_prev, cond_emb))
    return fca.total()

4) Training loop with unrolled K and distillation

def train_step(batch, model_r2diff, teacher_model, optimizer, K_min=2, K_max=6):
    imgs, texts = batch
    x_T, t_schedule, eps_gt = make_ddpm_training_batch(imgs)
    K = torch.randint(low=K_min, high=K_max+1, size=(1,)).item()
    s = torch.randint(low=0, high=len(t_schedule)-K, size=(1,)).item()
    t_unroll = t_schedule[s:s+K]
    loss_total = 0.0
    feats_q, scales, zps = None, None, None
    x = x_T
    for i, t in enumerate(t_unroll):
        t_embed = time_embed_fn(torch.tensor([t], device=x.device))
        cond_emb = global_embed_fn(x, t_embed, texts)
        if i == 0:
            feats_fp = model_r2diff.encoder.run_ote(x)
            feats_q, scales, zps = [], [], []
            for h in feats_fp:
                q, sc, zp = PerChannelUint8.quantize(h)
                feats_q.append(q); scales.append(sc); zps.append(zp)
        else:
            feats_q, scales, zps = model_r2diff.encoder.recurrent_update(feats_q, scales, zps, cond_emb)
        h_current = [PerChannelUint8.dequantize(q, sc.to(x.device), zp.to(x.device)).to(dtype=torch.float16)
                     for q,sc,zp in zip(feats_q, scales, zps)]
        eps_pred = model_r2diff.eps_head(model_r2diff.decoder(x, h_current), t_embed, texts)
        loss_eps = F.mse_loss(eps_pred, eps_gt[t])
        with torch.no_grad():
            eps_teacher = teacher_model(x, t, texts)
        loss_distill = F.mse_loss(eps_pred, eps_teacher)
        loss_total = loss_total + loss_eps + 0.25*loss_distill
        x = ddpm_forward_step(x, eps_gt[t], t)  # move to next noisy x
    optimizer.zero_grad(); loss_total.backward(); optimizer.step()
    return loss_total.item()

5) On-device latency (optional, Core ML)

import coremltools as ct

def export_to_coreml(torch_module, sample_input, fp16=True):
    traced = torch.jit.trace(torch_module, sample_input).eval()
    mlp = ct.convert(traced, inputs=[ct.TensorType(shape=sample_input.shape)], compute_units=ct.ComputeUnit.ALL)
    if fp16:
        mlp = ct.models.neural_network.quantization_utils.quantize_weights(mlp, nbits=16)
    mlp.save('r2diff_module.mlmodel')

----------------------------------------------------------------
How these experiments jointly validate R2Diff:
- Experiment 1 establishes the core claim: large speedups, lower memory and energy with negligible quality loss, and shows that learned γk and 8-bit state are effective in practice.
- Experiment 2 demonstrates sampler-agnosticism and backbone generality, and confirms compatibility with fast samplers (LCM) without trading off FID.
- Experiment 3 explains where the gains come from and which design choices matter, strengthening the causal link between the recurrent architecture and observed improvements.

Practical tips and feasibility notes:
- Start with 256×256 or 384×384 training crops to iterate quickly, then scale to 512×512 for SD1.5.
- Use gradient checkpointing only during initial OTE fine-tuning if memory-bound; inference needs none since recurrent Δ-updates are lightweight.
- Precompute COCO Inception stats for FID to speed evaluation. Use 3 seeds with subsets first (10k) before full 50k runs.
- To integrate with existing SD codebases, implement the encoder API returning multi-scale features and a decoder API accepting those features; R2Diff swaps only the encoder path from step 1 onward.

Expected outcomes (to verify):
- GPU: ~3.2× images/s, ~40–55% energy savings, and ~40% peak memory reduction vs UNet baseline on DDIM-25 with ≤0.15 FID delta.
- Learned γk prunes ≥60% Δ-FLOPs at high t; 8-bit state incurs <0.02 FID loss while lowering memory bandwidth ~30%.
- Few-step regime (≤8): R2Diff beats encoder-propagation and ASE by 0.5–1.0 FID.
- LCM-8: parity FID (e.g., 7.8 vs 7.9) with ~2× speedup from recurrent updates.
experimental_design.experiment_details:
Validating R2Diff: a time-recurrent diffusion backbone that eliminates per-step redundant computation

This document details three experiments that jointly validate speed, memory, energy, and quality of the proposed R2Diff method, its sampler-agnostic robustness across backbones, and the contribution of each component (Δ-blocks, state quantization, learned gating, distillation). All experiments target PyTorch implementations and reuse widely available libraries. Where multiple verification items can be addressed in one run, we integrate them to minimize redundancy while preserving rigor.

Common setup across experiments
- Codebase: Hugging Face diffusers for Stable Diffusion (SD1.5), timm for DiT, open_clip for CLIP, torch-fidelity for FID/precision/recall, fvcore for flops, pynvml for energy, accelerate for multi-GPU. Optional: deepspeed for large-scale training, coremltools for on-device evaluation.
- Hardware: A100-80GB primary; optionally A6000/4090 for cross-check; iPhone 14 Pro (Core ML) for mobile latency.
- Determinism: torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark=False, torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic=True, torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True) when feasible. Seed all RNGs per run and log seeds. Use identical noise schedules, prompts, CFG, and deterministic samplers across all model variants.
- Sampler configuration: diffusers.schedulers (DDIM, DDPM, DPM-Solver++). For LCM, use official LCM weights/scheduler.
- Logging: W&B or TensorBoard for loss curves, throughput, memory, power, γ statistics, Δ-FLOP pruning, and evaluation metrics. Save YAML configs and git commit hashes for reproducibility.
- Ethical/data hygiene: COCO val prompts only; LAION-Aesthetics filtered for NSFW using LAION metadata; deduplicate captions with SimHash; report dataset details.

---------------------------------------------
Experiment 1 — End-to-end speed, memory, energy, and quality on SD1.5 with DDIM-25

Hypotheses
- H1: R2Diff achieves ≥3× speedup on A100 at 512×512 with ≤0.15 FID delta vs baseline on DDIM-25.
- H2: Peak memory reduced by ≥40% and energy by ≥40% vs baseline.
- H3: Learned gating γk prunes >50% Δ-FLOPs for later timesteps; 8-bit state keeps FID loss <0.02 vs float state.

Models and data
- Base model: Stable Diffusion v1.5 (diffusers sd-v1-5). Same VAE and CLIP text encoder across variants.
- R2Diff modifications: One-Time Encoder (OTE) identical to UNet encoder at first step; Recurrent Δ-blocks (depthwise ConvGRU + FiLM) per scale with weight sharing across time; learned gating γk per layer; 8-bit per-channel state.
- Training data: LAION-Aesthetics subset (target 2M; feasibility start 200k–500k). Tokenization: CLIP-ViT-L/14 tokenize from open_clip.
- Evaluation prompts: MS-COCO 2014 val prompt set (30k). Additional 10k subset for quick pilots.

Training recipe (R2Diff)
- Loss: Sum of epsilon-pred MSE (or v-pred variant) across unrolled timesteps plus teacher forcing from frozen SD1.5 UNet.
- Unrolling: For each batch, sample K∈[2,6], start step s~U(0,T−K) and unroll K steps.
- Gating regularization: Add small sparsity prior λ·mean(γk) with λ warm-started to 0 and linearly ramped to 1e-3 by 30k steps to encourage pruning without over-suppressing early training.
- Optimizer: AdamW(lr=1e-4, β=(0.9, 0.95), wd=0.01), cosine LR, warmup 2k, mixed precision (bf16/amp). Batch size: 256 images (global), gradient accumulation if needed.
- Schedulers: Same noise schedule as baseline SD1.5. Teacher loss weight: 0.25 (ramp from 0.1→0.25 over first 10k steps). EMA of Δ-parameters (decay 0.999) for evaluation stability.
- Stabilization: Clip grad-norm (1.0). If any divergence is detected (loss spikes), temporarily cap γk to 0.8 and add gradient centralization in Δ-block 1×1 convs.

Evaluation protocol
- Primary sampler: DDIM-25, guidance scale 7.5. Secondary sampler: DDPM-50 (smaller slice) for reference.
- Metrics: FID (50k), CLIP score, precision/recall (Kynkäanniemi PR via torch-fidelity), throughput (images/s), latency per image, peak GPU memory, total GPU energy.
- Robustness slices: steps {8, 15, 25}, CFG {3, 7.5, 12} on 10k samples.
- Seeds: 3 seeds for generation; report mean±std. Use paired seeds across model variants for fair comparison.
- Mobile: export OTE and Δ-blocks to Core ML and measure per-image latency on iPhone 14 Pro for 512×512 with DDIM-25.

Baselines for comparison
- Original SD1.5 UNet (identical sampler/steps/CFG).
- Encoder propagation baseline (e.g., FasterDiffusion or similar open-source implementation) with its recommended settings.
- ASE and ToMe(0.4) applied to baseline UNet (ToMe on first pass to align with R2Diff’s OTE crunch).

Implementation details
- Integration with diffusers UNet2DConditionModel: split encoder/decoder by reusing down_blocks and up_blocks. Cache the shapes and feature indices expected by up_blocks. Replace subsequent down_blocks execution by Δ-updates of cached features.
- Feature hooks: in diffusers, up_blocks take residuals from down_blocks via a stack. We preserve that contract by feeding updated features at each timestep.

Example PyTorch components
1) Δ-blocks and FiLM conditioning (depthwise ConvGRU + FiLM)
```
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

class DepthwiseConvGRU(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, C, k=3):
        super().__init__()
        p = k//2
        self.conv_z = nn.Conv2d(C*2, C, k, padding=p, groups=C)
        self.conv_r = nn.Conv2d(C*2, C, k, padding=p, groups=C)
        self.conv_h = nn.Conv2d(C*2, C, k, padding=p, groups=C)
    def forward(self, x, h):
        if h is None:
            h = torch.zeros_like(x)
        xh = torch.cat([x, h], 1)
        z = torch.sigmoid(self.conv_z(xh))
        r = torch.sigmoid(self.conv_r(xh))
        rh = torch.cat([x, r*h], 1)
        h_tilde = torch.tanh(self.conv_h(rh))
        return (1 - z) * h + z * h_tilde

class FiLM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, C, d=1280):  # CLIP text + t-embed typical size
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 2*C), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(2*C, 2*C))
    def forward(self, x, cond):
        gamma, beta = self.net(cond).chunk(2, -1)
        return x * (1 + gamma[..., None, None]) + beta[..., None, None]

class DeltaBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, C, d_embed=1280, depth=1):
        super().__init__()
        self.grus = nn.ModuleList([DepthwiseConvGRU(C) for _ in range(depth)])
        self.film = FiLM(C, d_embed)
        self.out = nn.Conv2d(C, C, 1)
    def forward(self, h_prev, cond):
        h = h_prev
        for gru in self.grus:
            h = gru(h_prev, h)
        h = self.film(h, cond)
        return self.out(h)
```

2) Per-channel uint8 quantization with percentile clipping (more robust than min/max)
```
class PerChannelUint8:
    @staticmethod
    def _pct_range(x_flat, pct=0.999):
        lo = torch.quantile(x_flat, 1-pct, dim=0)
        hi = torch.quantile(x_flat, pct, dim=0)
        return lo, hi
    @staticmethod
    def quantize(x, pct=0.999):
        x = x.float()
        B,C,H,W = x.shape
        xf = x.permute(0,2,3,1).reshape(-1,C)
        lo, hi = PerChannelUint8._pct_range(xf, pct)
        scale = (hi - lo).clamp(min=1e-6) / 255.0
        zp = (-lo / scale).round().clamp(0,255)
        q = (x.permute(0,2,3,1) / scale - zp).round().clamp(0,255).to(torch.uint8)
        q = q.permute(0,3,1,2).contiguous()
        return q, scale, zp
    @staticmethod
    def dequantize(q, scale, zp):
        return (q.float() + zp[None,:,None,None]) * scale[None,:,None,None]
```

3) Learned time gating with sparsity prior
```
class TimeGating(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, d//2), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(d//2, 1), nn.Sigmoid())
    def forward(self, t_emb):  # (B, d)
        return self.net(t_emb).view(-1,1,1,1)
```

4) R2Diff encoder wrapper for diffusers UNet down_blocks
```
class R2DiffEncoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, down_blocks, ch_layout, d_embed=1280, depth=1):
        super().__init__()
        self.ote = down_blocks  # list of original down_blocks
        self.deltas = nn.ModuleList([DeltaBlock(C, d_embed, depth) for C in ch_layout])
        self.gates = nn.ModuleList([TimeGating(d_embed) for _ in ch_layout])

    @torch.no_grad()
    def run_ote(self, x, t_emb, text_cond):
        feats = []
        h = x
        for db in self.ote:
            h, res = db(h, temb=t_emb, encoder_hidden_states=text_cond)
            # collect feature to match skip order expected by up_blocks
            feats.extend(res)
        return feats

    def quantize_feats(self, feats):
        feats_q, scales, zps = [], [], []
        for f in feats:
            q, sc, zp = PerChannelUint8.quantize(f)
            feats_q.append(q); scales.append(sc); zps.append(zp)
        return feats_q, scales, zps

    def recurrent_update(self, feats_q, scales, zps, cond_emb):
        new_q, new_sc, new_zp = [], [], []
        for (q, sc, zp, db, gate) in zip(feats_q, scales, zps, self.deltas, self.gates):
            h = PerChannelUint8.dequantize(q, sc.to(q.device), zp.to(q.device)).to(torch.float16)
            delta = db(h, cond_emb) * gate(cond_emb)
            h_new = (h + delta).to(torch.float32)
            q2, sc2, zp2 = PerChannelUint8.quantize(h_new)
            new_q.append(q2); new_sc.append(sc2); new_zp.append(zp2)
        return new_q, new_sc, new_zp
```

5) Measurement utilities (latency, energy, peak memory)
```
import time, pynvml, torch

def measure_run(fn, *args, warmup=3, repeat=10):
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    for _ in range(warmup): fn(*args); torch.cuda.synchronize()
    times, energies = [], []
    pynvml.nvmlInit(); handle = pynvml.nvmlDeviceGetHandleByIndex(0)
    try:
        for _ in range(repeat):
            torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
            t0 = time.time()
            e0 = pynvml.nvmlDeviceGetTotalEnergyConsumption(handle)  # mJ if supported
            fn(*args); torch.cuda.synchronize()
            e1 = pynvml.nvmlDeviceGetTotalEnergyConsumption(handle)
            t1 = time.time()
            times.append(t1-t0)
            energies.append(max(0.0, (e1-e0)/1000.0))  # J
            peak_mem = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()/(1024**2)
    finally:
        pynvml.nvmlShutdown()
    return dict(latency_ms_mean=1000*sum(times)/len(times),
                latency_ms_std=1000*torch.tensor(times).std().item(),
                energy_j_mean=sum(energies)/len(energies),
                peak_mem_mb=peak_mem)
```

```
def compute_clip_score(imgs, texts, model="ViT-L-14"):
    model, _, preprocess = open_clip.create_model_and_transforms(model, pretrained="openai")
    model = model.eval().cuda()
    with torch.no_grad():
```

```
class TokenDeltaBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, C, d_embed=512, depth=1):
        super().__init__()
        self.grus = nn.ModuleList([nn.GRU(input_size=C, hidden_size=C, num_layers=1, batch_first=True) for _ in range(depth)])
        self.film = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d_embed, 2*C), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(2*C, 2*C))
        self.out = nn.Linear(C, C)
    def forward(self, h_prev, cond):  # h_prev: (B, N, C)
        h = h_prev
        for gru in self.grus:
            h,_ = gru(h, h.transpose(0,1).contiguous().unsqueeze(0))  # use prev as init; light sharing
        gamma, beta = self.film(cond).chunk(2, -1)
        h = h * (1 + gamma[:,None,:]) + beta[:,None,:]
        return self.out(h)
```

Key helpers
1) 4-bit quantization option
```
class PerChannelUint4:
    @staticmethod
    def quantize(x, pct=0.999):
        x = x.float()
        B,C,H,W = x.shape
        xf = x.permute(0,2,3,1).reshape(-1,C)
        lo = torch.quantile(xf, 1-pct, dim=0)
        hi = torch.quantile(xf, pct, dim=0)
        scale = (hi - lo).clamp(min=1e-6) / 15.0
        zp = (-lo / scale).round().clamp(0,15)
        q = (x.permute(0,2,3,1) / scale - zp).round().clamp(0,15).to(torch.uint8)
        return q, scale, zp
    @staticmethod
    def dequantize(q, scale, zp):
        return (q.float() + zp[None,:,None,None]) * scale[None,:,None,None]
```

4) Training loop with K-unroll and teacher forcing (sketch)
```
def train_step(batch, model_r2diff, teacher_model, optimizer, sched):
    imgs, texts = batch
    x_T, t_schedule, eps_gt = make_ddpm_training_batch(imgs)  # reuse baseline utilities
    K = torch.randint(2, 7, (1,)).item()
    s = torch.randint(0, len(t_schedule)-K, (1,)).item()
    t_unroll = t_schedule[s:s+K]
    loss_total = 0.0
    feats_q = scales = zps = None
    x = x_T
    for i, t in enumerate(t_unroll):
        temb = time_embed_fn(torch.tensor([t], device=x.device))
        cond_emb = global_embed_fn(x, temb, texts)
        if i == 0:
            feats = model_r2diff.encoder.run_ote(x, temb, text_cond=encode_text(texts))
            feats_q, scales, zps = model_r2diff.encoder.quantize_feats(feats)
        else:
            feats_q, scales, zps = model_r2diff.encoder.recurrent_update(feats_q, scales, zps, cond_emb)
        h_current = [PerChannelUint8.dequantize(q, sc.to(x.device), zp.to(x.device)).to(torch.float16)
                     for q, sc, zp in zip(feats_q, scales, zps)]
        eps_pred = model_r2diff.eps_head(model_r2diff.decoder(x, h_current), temb, encode_text(texts))
        loss_eps = F.mse_loss(eps_pred, eps_gt[t])
        with torch.no_grad(): eps_teacher = teacher_model(x, t, texts)
        loss_distill = F.mse_loss(eps_pred, eps_teacher)
        gamma_sparsity = sum([g(temb).mean() for g in model_r2diff.encoder.gates]) / len(model_r2diff.encoder.gates)
        loss_total = loss_total + loss_eps + 0.25*loss_distill + 1e-3*gamma_sparsity
        x = ddpm_forward_step(x, eps_gt[t], t)
    optimizer.zero_grad(); loss_total.backward(); optimizer.step()
    sched.step()
    return loss_total.item()
```

Reliability and analysis

- Plot γk vs timestep to visualize adaptive budget. Confirm that learned gating achieves ≥60% Δ-FLOP pruning for t > 0.7T.

Shared implementation notes and reproducibility checklist
- Diffusers split: Create a subclass of UNet2DConditionModel that exposes down_blocks forward and accepts externally supplied residuals for up_blocks. Keep attention processor identical to baseline.
- Global embedding: Concatenate sinusoidal time embedding and pooled CLIP text embedding, project to d_embed with a small MLP. For CFG, pass unconditional and conditional embeddings separately if using classifier-free guidance; Δ-blocks receive the conditional branch embedding.
- Mixed precision: Use torch.autocast(bf16) whenever possible to reduce memory bandwidth.
- DDP/Accelerate: Use accelerate launch for multi-GPU training; set gradient accumulation to keep per-GPU memory under control.
- Artifacts: Save checkpoints every N steps with EMA. Save evaluation CSVs with sampler, steps, CFG, seed, FID, CLIP, PR, images/s, J/img, peak MB.
- Statistical significance: Report 95% CI for FID via bootstrap; paired t-test for CLIP and PR across seeds; confirm effect sizes for speed and memory are well beyond measurement noise (repeat 10–20 times for latency/energy measurement).

---------------------------------------------
Expected outcomes to verify
- Exp1: ~3.2× images/s, 40–55% energy reduction, ~40% peak memory reduction vs UNet baseline at DDIM-25 with ≤0.15 FID delta; learned γk prunes ≥60% Δ-FLOPs at high t; int8 state incurs <0.02 FID loss while lowering bandwidth ~30%.
- Exp2: Sampler-agnostic parity at 25 steps; improved few-step FID (≤8 steps) vs encoder-propagation and ASE; with LCM-8, parity FID (e.g., 7.8 vs 7.9) and ≥2× faster. DiT-XL/2 on ImageNet-256: parity FID under DDPM-50 with ≥3× speedup.

By executing these three integrated experiments, we rigorously validate that R2Diff eliminates per-step redundant computation via native time recurrence, achieves multi-fold speedups with negligible quality loss, remains sampler/backbone agnostic, and provides clear causal attribution for each architectural component.
